question: Why is columnar storage preferred over row-based storage for analytical warehouse workloads?
options: It makes single-row inserts and updates dramatically faster
It guarantees stronger transactional consistency than row storage
It lets queries read only the columns they need and compresses similar values well
It stores each row contiguously to speed up point lookups
explanation: Columnar layout stores each column together, so analytical queries scan only the needed columns and benefit from high compression of similar values, cutting I/O dramatically.

question: What does MPP (Massively Parallel Processing) architecture do in a data warehouse?
options: Splits data across many nodes and processes query fragments in parallel, then combines results
Runs the entire query on one large CPU core for consistency
Processes queries strictly sequentially to avoid data conflicts
Stores all data in RAM on a single machine
explanation: MPP distributes data and query work across many nodes that compute in parallel and merge results, enabling fast processing of huge datasets.

question: Columnar storage typically achieves better compression than row storage mainly because:
options: Columns are stored in random order to confuse the compressor
Row storage cannot be compressed at all
Compression only works on integer data types
Values within a single column are of the same type and often similar, aiding encoding
explanation: Since a column holds homogeneous, often-repeating values of one data type, techniques like run-length and dictionary encoding compress it very effectively.

question: In an MPP system, a query that requires shuffling large amounts of data between nodes (e.g., a join on a non-distributed key) is slow primarily because of:
options: Excessive CPU cache misses on a single node
The cost of network data movement (redistribution) across nodes
Columnar compression being disabled during joins
The lack of any parallelism in MPP systems
explanation: Data redistribution (shuffle) moves rows across the network so matching keys land on the same node; heavy shuffles are a common MPP performance bottleneck.

question: For a query 'SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees' on a wide 200-column table, columnar storage is faster because:
options: It only reads the salary column from storage, skipping the other 199
It reads all 200 columns but ignores 199 of them in memory
It converts the table to rows first for the aggregation
It requires a full index scan of every column
explanation: Columnar storage lets the engine read only the salary column from disk, avoiding I/O on the unneeded 199 columns, a major win for wide-table analytics.
